bullets: How place value decides what each digit is worth, how to add and subtract with regrouping, and why multiplication is repeated addition
slides.heading: Whole numbers: place value, adding, subtracting, multiplying
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we work with whole numbers - place value, adding, subtracting and multiplying - and by the end you will be able to explain why the zero in 5 0 6 7 matters so much.

bullets: Read any whole number by naming the thousands, hundreds, tens and ones places
Add and subtract column by column, regrouping when a column overflows or runs short
Explain multiplication as repeated addition of equal groups
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: A shop sign reads 5 0 6 7 stickers in stock - but a classmate reads it as 567
How many stickers are really there, and what difference does one small zero make?
slides.heading: Five thousand stickers, or five hundred?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands: 567 or five thousand and sixty-seven? Take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: hold on to your idea, because scene s6 settles this exactly.

bullets: A digit is worth its face value times its place: the same 5 means 5000 in the thousands place and 5 in the ones place
When a column reaches ten, regroup: ten of one place become one of the next place up
slides.heading: Place value decides what a digit is worth
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: where a digit stands decides what it is worth, and regrouping is just trading ten small pieces for one bigger piece of equal value.

bullets: Write 3 452 and name each place: 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 5 tens, 2 ones
Ten ones regroup into one ten - the first regrouping move of the lesson
slides.heading: Thousands, hundreds, tens, ones
slides.notes: Point at the columns as the digits drop in and narrate: watch the ten ones dots gather and become one ten-chip - nothing was added, the same amount changed shape.

bullets: Ones first: 7 + 5 = 12, so write 2 in the ones and carry 1 ten
Tens next: 4 + 8 + 1 carried = 13, so write 3 and carry 1 hundred; hundreds: 2 + 3 + 1 = 6
slides.heading: Addition with regrouping: 247 + 385
slides.notes: Count aloud with the class at each regrouping: twelve ones become one ten and two ones, thirteen tens become one hundred and three tens. The answer is 632.

bullets: Ones: 2 is too few to take 7, so borrow one ten and the ones become 12; 12 take away 7 is 5
Tens: 2 is too few to take 4, so borrow one hundred and the tens become 12; 12 take away 4 is 8; hundreds: 5 take away 2 is 3
slides.heading: Subtraction with regrouping: 632 − 247
slides.notes: Narrate both borrows slowly: each borrow trades one bigger piece for ten smaller ones, so the total never changes - only the shape of the number changes. The answer is 385.

bullets: Four groups of three dots gather into one array of twelve
Counting the array gives 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, which is what 4 x 3 means
slides.heading: Multiplication is repeated addition
slides.notes: Watch the four groups slide together into the array, then follow the counting probe dot by dot: multiplication is just a shortcut for adding the same group again and again.

bullets: Start with 45 stickers, add 25 more to reach 70, then give 30 away to land on 40
Work left to right: 45 + 25 = 70, then 70 - 30 = 40
slides.heading: One worked example: 45 + 25 − 30
slides.notes: Talk through the tens blocks and ones dots as they arrive and leave: first the total grows to 70 with ten ones regrouped into a ten, then three tens leave and 40 remains.

bullets: The trap claim in full: Reading 5 0 6 7 as 567, skipping the zero.
Zero holds its place: 5 0 6 7 is five thousand and sixty-seven, with the 0 keeping the hundreds empty
slides.heading: Misconception: the zero in 5 0 6 7 holds its place
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud: Reading 5 0 6 7 as 567, skipping the zero. Then land the correction: Zero holds its place: 5 0 6 7 is five thousand and sixty-seven, with the 0 keeping the hundreds empty.

bullets: Work 45 + 25 - 30 in two steps: first 45 + 25 = 70, then 70 - 30 = 40
Check each step with place value: 4 tens and 5 ones, then 7 tens, then 4 tens
slides.heading: Worked example: 45 + 25 − 30
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly as in scene s5 and name each one as you write it; say: doing one operation at a time, left to right, keeps every place honest.

bullets: Work out 247 + 385 on your whiteboards, regrouping in the ones and the tens
Careful - a classmate says: Reading 5 0 6 7 as 567, skipping the zero. Correct them in one sentence, naming what the zero does
slides.heading: Your turn: add, then judge the claim
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on where each carried ten and hundred came from first, then on the exact sentence they used to correct the claim: Reading 5 0 6 7 as 567, skipping the zero.

bullets: On your own: work out 632 - 247, showing both borrows
Watch out for the trap one last time: Reading 5 0 6 7 as 567, skipping the zero. Say what 5 0 6 7 really is, and what the zero is doing
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for both borrows in your first answer, plus one clear sentence about the zero holding its place in your second.
